name: Deep voice masculinity meta

lead: This forum framework holds that a lower pitch signals masculinity and dominance, giving a stronger presence and higher perceived attractiveness and status.

Pitch is set by vocal fold length, mass and tension. Adult male folds are longer and thicker, giving a lower pitch on average: typical speech is about 90 to 155 Hz for males and 165 to 255 Hz for females. The sources reviewed document these voice differences but not the social effects.

paras: Followers focus on lowering how their voice sounds, through things like speaking lower in the natural range, recording setups or other voice-focused tactics covered elsewhere on the wiki.
Attempts to deepen the voice by straining or using irritants carry vocal health risks, and straining is described as a cause of vocal injury.

web.title: PubMed search results: male voice pitch attractiveness dominance

angle.text: Forums hold that a deeper voice reads as more masculine and dominant, adding to attractiveness and status. Voice physiology is well described, while the social-perception claim circulates mostly as anecdote.

lead: The deep voice masculinity meta is the belief, found in looksmaxxing and related culture, that a lower voice pitch signals masculinity and dominance and so adds to how attractive, authoritative or high-status a man comes across. In this framing the voice is treated as part of a man's overall presence, alongside face, frame and posture, and a deeper voice is seen as a trait that improves how he is perceived.

Typical fundamental frequencies for adult speech are about 90 to 155 Hz for males and 165 to 255 Hz for females.[1] Adult male vocal folds are longer and thicker than female folds, which usually produces a lower pitch, and a larger male vocal tract also lowers timbre.[2][3]

Psychology and evolutionary-biology researchers have studied the idea directly. Wikipedia's article on voice pitch reports that pitch is related to interpersonal power, that Darwin proposed the male-female difference arose through sexual selection, and that studies found women favouring lower male voices mainly for short-term relationships.[4] Papers listed in PubMed describe pitch as strongly linked to perceived attractiveness and dominance, with evidence for links to actual fighting ability described as sparse and mixed.[5]
infobox: Voice pitch, attractiveness and dominance perception[4][5]

paras: Pitch is shaped mainly by vocal fold length, size and tension. Averages are given as about 125 Hz for adult males and 210 Hz for adult females.[3] Conditions that add mass to the folds, such as Reinke's edema, lower the fundamental frequency.[3] Wikipedia's voice pitch article notes that male voices remain lower than female voices even after body height and volume are accounted for.[4]
Proponents hold that a deeper voice conveys dominance and masculine status. Encyclopedic sources note that voice can reveal speaker age and sex and convey emotion.[2]

sections.h: Research on pitch, attractiveness and dominance
paras: Wikipedia reports that Charles Darwin proposed the male-female pitch difference arose through sexual selection driven largely by female mate choice, that women's preference for male pitch shifted across the menstrual cycle, and that women favoured lower male voices mainly for short-term relationships. It adds that pitch is related to interpersonal power and that men adjust their pitch according to how dominant they perceive a competitor to be.[4]

PubMed-listed studies include a 2016 Behavioral Ecology paper arguing that lower-pitched voices and beards may have evolved mainly through competition between men, a 2011 British Journal of Psychology study linking women's stronger preference for low pitch in short-term partners to how physically dominant they perceive men to be, a 2012 PLoS One paper on preference for leaders with masculine voices, a 2020 Scientific Reports study of 160 men relating vocal parameters to perception, body morphology, strength and hormones, a 2021 paper on voice pitch in amateur fighters, and a 2023 Scientific Reports paper reporting that pitch and other acoustic features affect perceived attractiveness, status and formidability, with hypotheses partly supported.[5]
No clinical trials found of interventions to deepen the voice for appearance. Observational and perception studies of voice pitch, attractiveness and dominance are summarised above.[4][5]
